quote: Awesome. And I have you done as the property owner here, Dominic. Is there anyone else on the title?
stewart_read: Rep correctly runs the title co-owner verify item and captures that the wife is on title. This is not an objection-shaped moment (no protocols.spouse_decision trigger phrase occurred), so it's best read as verify-item execution, not protocol handling.
alternative_hypothesis: Could be read as an early protocol trigger, but no spousal objection or hesitation language appears here — it's a straight qualification question.
coaching_implication: Good baseline execution; the follow-through gap is later, at 04:24, when the customer volunteers he wants his wife present and the rep doesn't explicitly confirm her attendance for the phone appointment.

quote: I would definitely want to be want to be there, you know, obviously, and not just my wife. You know what I mean?
stewart_read: Customer explicitly names his wife as someone who should also be involved, going beyond the earlier title disclosure into an attendance statement. Rep responds with 'Sure. 100%.' and moves the conversation to scheduling mechanics rather than confirming she'll be on the call.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged this as the customer simply asserting his own presence (not raising a co-decider concern), which would make a hard confirmation unnecessary in the moment.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to close the loop explicitly: a one-line 'Let's make sure she's on the call with us too' would lock the co-owner in per protocol, rather than leaving her attendance ambiguous going into the closer call.

quote: Our most recent bill, I think, was, like, $2.02 42 or something like that. I just opened it this morning, which is kinda what prompted the whole conversation.
stewart_read: Customer hands the rep both the dollar figure and the emotional trigger (opening the bill this morning is literally why he called) in the same breath. Rep responds with only 'Oh, gotcha. Okay. Gotcha.' and moves to the next verify item without reflecting the bill back as leverage.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may be intentionally saving the emotional flip for later in the call when discussing the design, rather than spending it immediately mid-verify — but no such later flip actually occurs in the transcript.
coaching_implication: This is the clearest missed flip on the call: the customer literally narrated his own bill-pain trigger. A line like reflecting the bill amount back as the reason solar is worth a look would have used the moment instead of filing it.

quote: does 1,200 kilowatts a month sound, like, normal?
stewart_read: Customer volunteers a specific usage number unprompted and asks a comparative question — a natural curiosity hook. Rep answers factually ('a little bit more on the higher side') and pivots to needing the actual bill, which is a reasonable, schema-aligned redirect for accuracy, not a processing failure, but the rep doesn't use the number to build anticipation about what the design might show.
alternative_hypothesis: The redirect to the bill for '100% accurate numbers' is itself schema-correct (curiosity_over_features discourages guessing at savings), so this may be sound procedure rather than a missed opportunity.
coaching_implication: Minor: the rep could pair the accurate-numbers redirect with a curiosity line about what the design will reveal, but the core response was procedurally fine and shouldn't be treated as a rep intent failure.

quote: I I don't want the expectation to be like, oh, yeah. We're we're gonna, you know, tell them as soon as we get them on the phone type of deal.
stewart_read: Customer sets an explicit boundary that the appointment is exploratory, not a commitment signal. Rep validates this cleanly ('This is just for you to... see if it's a good fit') without pressuring, which is the correct protocol response rather than treating it as an objection to overcome.
coaching_implication: Nothing to fix here — flag for the closer's handoff brief so they don't walk in assuming high purchase intent.

quote: I I guess one question is, is this like a a lease thing, or do we own the panels, or how how does how does that wall work?
stewart_read: This is a closer-tier financial-mechanism question. Rep's response ('there's different options... they'll be able to go over everything') correctly redirects to the specialist instead of explaining lease vs. purchase himself.
alternative_hypothesis: Could be graded as a knowledge_gap if the rep didn't know the answer, but the phrasing shows a deliberate redirect rather than an admission of not knowing.
coaching_implication: This is a positive example worth playing back to other reps — clean use of the scope escape hatch under a direct product question.

quote: Well, yeah, I mean, from what it looks like, it looks like a great home for solar. I mean, you don't have any super tall trees in the way.
stewart_read: Rep notes favorable roof/tree conditions via Google Maps, a positive qualifying observation, but doesn't tie it back to anything the customer can get excited about beyond a passing comment.
coaching_implication: Minor upside: reps can turn 'good home for solar' observations into a forward-pulling hook (e.g., tying it to what the design will likely show) rather than a flat qualifying statement.
